(1) Deibler 1976, A Gahuku-Yaweyuha comparative grammar (image-only scan; I read the rendered page images the page image and directly, not just the scanned). Typescript p.3, section 2 'Phonology': "Each language has two phonemic register tones, each syllable carrying one of the tones^3. Non-verbal Morph…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yaweyuha is described as a register-tone language (two tones, H and L, one per syllable; Potts et al. 1974 tentatively add a rising tone on a few monosyllables), with very low functional load. The author states explicitly that word-stress patterns have not been analysed; no stress placement rule exists in any of the three SIL descriptions.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 3: in syllables containing two vowels the tone of the second vowel may differ from the first. Potts, James & Deibler 1974 (4.5): high tone has a down-glide allotone on the final syllable of final verbs; general downdrift over an utterance. OPD 1992: tone not written, very low functional load.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is assigned per syllable of the (phonological) word; the stress remark refers to 'phonological words'. No phrase-level prosody beyond downdrift is described.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources describe Yaweyuha (also called Yabiyufa), ISO yby = Glottolog yawe1241; 1974 data from speakers of Apoeto village (Unggai census division, Goroka sub-district). The 1976 source is a Gahuku-Yaweyuha comparison; the quoted sentences refer to Yaweyuha specifically (tone statement covers both languages).

new_statements.quote: [p. 7] There has not been time to do an analysis of the tone system of Yaweyuha, and the conclusions contained herein and even the tones marked on examples are highly tentative. Rising tone has been noted on very few words, most of them monosyllabic, but it seems to contrast with both high and low. [p. 8, sec. 4.5] High tone /´/ has a down glide allotone [⌐] which occurs on the final syllable of final verbs. All tonemes have higher allotones at the beginning of a stream of speech, which become progressively lower as speech continues due to a general lowering of the entire voice register during the course of normal speech events. [p. 10, sec. 6.2] As phonemic norms, except that we propose not to write tone. To date only 11 minimal pairs have been noted

Read the page images the page image, and the scanned of p. 10 (the page image; my own page render render was queued behind the project wrapper and never returned, so I used the images already held by the project). p. 7 image, first paragraph, reads exactly: 'There has not been time to do an analysis of the tone system of Yaweyuha, and the conclusions contained herein and even the tones marked on examples are highly tentative. Rising tone has been noted on very few words, most of them monosyllabic, but it seems to contrast with both high and low.' p. 8 imag…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing statement from Deibler 1976 (tone language, no stress statement): this earlier 1974 paper by the same SIL team also treats Yaweyuha as a register-tone language and says nothing about stress. It differs in detail only on the tone inventory (three tones incl. a tentative rising tone vs the two register tones of Deibler 1976 and the OPD), which is a tone question, not a stress question.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper is a phoneme inventory with a tentative tone analysis: three tones are charted (high, low, rising; p. 2) with minimal pairs for high vs low, low vs rising and high vs rising (p. 6, sec. 3.3); high tone has a down-glide allotone on the final syllable of final verbs and all tones drift downward through an utterance (p. 8). The words 'stress', 'accent' and 'prominence' do not occur anywhere in the ten pages; there is no statement on where word stress falls or whether it exists.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone analysis explicitly 'highly tentative'; rising tone attested on very few, mostly monosyllabic words; only 11 tonal minimal pairs noted, so the authors propose not to write tone. Nothing on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The 1974 paper's data come from two speakers (Donney Belalo, 18, and Phillip Wanopa, 19) of Apoeto village, Ungai census division, Goroka sub-district, Eastern Highlands (p. 1); no dialect is distinguished. The language is called Yaweyuha throughout (= Yabiyufa, ISO yby).
